demo_steps.title: Printed figure
demo_steps.narration: The view begins by matching the printed source: green x = 1, red y = -2, blue z = 2, and the point label (1, -1, 2). No warning or correction annotation is shown in the default view.

demo_steps.title: One equation gives a plane
demo_steps.narration: Isolating the green sheet shows that x = 1 fixes only the x-coordinate. The y- and z-directions are still free, so the solution set is an entire plane.

demo_steps.title: Two equations meet in a line
demo_steps.narration: Adding the red sheet shows how two perpendicular coordinate planes intersect. Their shared points form a line before the third equation is applied.

demo_steps.title: Three planes locate one point
demo_steps.narration: Restoring the blue horizontal sheet gives a single common crossing point, which is the geometric meaning of solving three independent linear equations in three variables.

demo_steps.title: Optional consistency check
demo_steps.narration: Switching to a corrected label version shows how the marked point can be made to satisfy all three displayed equations, without changing the default reproduction of the source figure.

plan.geometry_notes: Use a right-handed coordinate system with z vertical. Do not draw coordinate axes, grid lines, tick marks, or a warning badge. Center the composition on the apparent crossing near world point (1, -2, 2). Model the planes as finite rectangles: green x = 1 plane has dimensions 5.6 units along world y by 4.8 units along world z, spanning y from -4.8 to 0.8 and z from -0.4 to 4.4; red y = -2 plane has dimensions 5.6 units along world x by 4.8 units along world z, spanning x from -1.8 to 3.8 and z from -0.4 to 4.4; blue z = 2 plane has dimensions 5.6 units along world x by 5.6 units along world y, spanning x from -1.8 to 3.8 and y from -4.8 to 0.8. Position and orientation: green plane is an upright yz-rectangle at x=1 and should read as the foremost broad upright parallelogram, leaning lower-left to upper-right on screen; red plane is an upright xz-rectangle at y=-2 and should read as a narrower tall diamond/parallelogram angled the opposite way, passing behind the left side of the green plane and reappearing on the right; blue plane is an xy-rectangle at z=2 and should read nearly horizontal, crossing left-to-right through the middle and slicing both vertical sheets. For the source-like default axonometric view, use an orthographic camera equivalent to looking from approximately world direction (5, -7, 4) toward (1, -2, 2), with a slight top-down elevation so the blue plane appears as a shallow horizontal parallelogram and the green plane remains visually dominant. Draw planes double-sided with saturated colors and opacity 0.82 to 0.9: green #22b14c, red #e01f26, blue #0077b6. Use darker outlines: green #0b7f2a, red #a80f17, blue #00517f. The overlap should be depth-sorted or stencil-split so pieces alternately hide one another rather than blending into muddy colors. Place the black point as a small sphere of radius about 0.07 at the visual crossing of all three planes. In the printed default label version, the point text must read exactly '(1, -1, 2)' even though the plotted intersection corresponds geometrically to (1, -2, 2). The leader line should run from the point upward and slightly right to the coordinate label. Put the green 'x = 1' label in green just outside the upper-right edge/tip of the green plane, not over the plane face. Put the red 'y = -2' label in red below the drawing, centered under the red sheet. Put the blue 'z = 2' label in blue just outside the right edge of the blue plane.
plan.notes: Render as an orthographic axonometric 3D scene with transparent, double-sided polygon planes. The constructionStage state should control visibility only: printedFigure and allThreePlanes both show all planes and labels; xPlaneOnly shows only the green plane and its label while dimming or hiding the point; xAndYPlanes shows green and red planes with their intersection line subtly emphasized; allThreePlanes shows all planes and the point. The labelVersion toggle must not create any default warning text. In 'Printed source', show exactly x = 1, y = -2, z = 2, and (1, -1, 2). In 'Correct red label to y = -1', change only the red equation text to y = -1 and keep the point label (1, -1, 2). In 'Correct point to (1, -2, 2)', keep the red label y = -2 and change only the coordinate label to (1, -2, 2). Clicking a plane or matching label should brighten that plane and outline it; any explanatory badge should be small and tied to the selected plane only, not a global conflict warning.

authoredPrompt: This figure shows three mutually perpendicular planes cutting through one another, drawn as flat colored parallelograms with no coordinate axes displayed. A green plane stands roughly upright facing the viewer, labeled x = 1 in matching green at its upper right. A red plane meets it at a right angle, tilted so it reads as a tall diamond passing behind and around the green sheet, labeled y = -2 in red beneath the drawing. A blue plane lies nearly horizontal and slices through both others, labeled z = 2 in blue at its right edge. The sheets overlap so each is partly hidden by the others, giving a sectioned, interlocking block in which the visible pieces alternate in color where they cross. A small black dot near the center is labeled (1, -1, 2), which conflicts with the red plane label y = -2; as drawn, the displayed point does not satisfy all three displayed plane equations. The drawing still gives geometric meaning to a system of three linear equations in three variables, but the plane label or point label must be corrected before the marked point can be treated as the simultaneous solution.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle individual planes on and off: the learner shows x = 1, y = -2, and z = 2 one at a time or together, while a warning highlights that the displayed point label (1, -1, 2) does not satisfy the red plane y = -2.
- Click for a plane label: the learner clicks a colored equation and its plane plus the coordinate it fixes are highlighted, making clear how each equation restricts one coordinate while leaving a full sheet of possible points.
- Toggle corrected-label overlay: the learner switches between the figure as printed and a corrected version, either y = -1 with point (1, -1, 2) or y = -2 with point (1, -2, 2), making clear that a solution must satisfy every plane equation simultaneously.
authoredContext:
The solution is the ordered triple (1,−1,2). See the figure.

An illustration of three orthogonal planes, x=1 (green), y=-2 (red), and z=2 (blue), intersecting at the labeled point (1, -1, 2) in a 3D coordinate system.

interactions.label: Show y plane

demo_steps.title: Printed figure
demo_steps.narration: All three planes are visible as in the source figure. The black point is labeled (1, -1, 2), but the red plane is labeled y = -2, so the warning marks the inconsistency.

demo_steps.title: Isolate one equation
demo_steps.narration: Show only the green plane. The equation x = 1 restricts one coordinate while leaving a whole plane of possible y- and z-values.

demo_steps.title: Planes intersect to locate a point
demo_steps.narration: Restore all three sheets. Their common intersection represents the ordered triple that satisfies all three equations.

demo_steps.title: Correct the inconsistency
demo_steps.narration: Switch to a corrected label. Either the red equation must be y = -1 for the printed point, or the point must be labeled (1, -2, 2) for the printed red equation.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a right-handed coordinate system with z vertical. The marked common point should be near the visual center. Model the three sheets as finite axis-aligned rectangles: green plane x = 1 spanning y from -4.2 to 1.6 and z from -0.4 to 4.2; red plane y = -2 spanning x from -1.8 to 4.0 and z from -0.4 to 4.2; blue plane z = 2 spanning x from -1.8 to 4.0 and y from -4.2 to 1.6. Each plane is roughly 5.8 units wide in each free coordinate. The point for the printed source geometry is drawn at the visual intersection of the three planes; mathematically this corresponds to (1, -2, 2), while the printed coordinate text reads (1, -1, 2). Colors: green #2fb84a for x = 1, red #e51b23 for y = -2, blue #057fa3 for z = 2, black #000000 for the point and leader line. Plane opacity should be high, about 0.88 to 0.95, so overlaps remain vivid but depth ordering is legible. The green plane should appear as the upright sheet running lower-left to upper-right, the red plane as the upright sheet slanting upper-left to lower-right behind it, and the blue plane as the almost horizontal sheet crossing left-to-right through the middle. Place the green label x = 1 just beyond the upper-right tip of the green plane, the blue label z = 2 just beyond the right edge of the blue plane, the red label y = -2 centered below the red sheet, and the coordinate label above and to the right of the black point with a thin leader line.
interactionPlan.notes: Render in orthographic axonometric/isometric style with no coordinate axes, matching the source. Use double-sided plane materials. For the clicked-label interaction, make the equation text meshes or HTML labels pickable; clicking a label should brighten the corresponding plane, add a darker outline around it, and display a small coordinate badge such as x fixed, y and z free. The individual plane toggles should hide both the plane and its matching label, but keep the central point and warning visible when the currently selected label version is inconsistent. In the corrected-label toggle, the 'Correct red label to y = -1' state changes only the red text and removes the warning; the 'Correct point to (1, -2, 2)' state changes only the coordinate text and removes the warning.

discrepancies: The generated figure adds a warning label and explanatory badge/UI about a printed-label conflict that are not present in the source image and visually distract from the textbook figure.
The black point is geometrically placed at the intersection for y = -2 while the visible coordinate label says (1, −1, 2), making the rendered geometry and label inconsistent in the default view.
The camera/view and plane proportions differ: the green x = 1 plane is too front-facing and dominant compared with the more balanced oblique overlap in the source.
The plane colors are more transparent and blended than the saturated opaque-looking red, green, and blue planes in the source.
The x = 1 label is poorly placed on/behind the green plane rather than clearly outside the plane edge as in the source.
evaluation.notes: The three intersecting colored planes and labeled point are recognizable, but the added inconsistency-warning concept, altered view, and default point/label mismatch reduce fidelity to the source.
action_items: Remove the warning label and conflict-explanation badge from the default view so the rendered figure matches the source image.
Use the printed source labels directly by default without adding corrective commentary unless hidden behind an optional teaching toggle.
Adjust the camera/view so the green, red, and blue planes have overlap and apparent angles closer to the source.
Increase color saturation/opacity and reposition the x = 1 label outside the green plane edge for clearer resemblance.
plan_action_items: Do not reinterpret the source as an error-correction figure by default; the primary plan should reproduce the printed figure first, with any correction feature optional and secondary.

feedback.rationale: The main fidelity issue is a plan-level reinterpretation of the source as an error-correction/teaching figure, causing hallucinated warning UI and commentary that the generator should not implement by default.
